# judgment

> Typed, calibrated judgments from TypeSafe System One models (Jev) and compatible backends, as a Rust crate.

This index is generated from the crate's documentation nav (`mkdocs.yml`) and each page's frontmatter by `scripts/gen-llms-txt.sh`; the pages are the source of truth. Read the README first: it says why the crate exists, what it guarantees and how it compares with the other Rust clients for the same wire. Then How judgment works for the mechanisms, What is in the crate for the modules, Patterns for TypeSafe's four patterns mapped onto the types with one runnable example each, Testing without the model for the fake and the recordings, The .jud format for the YAML documents that keep a rubric with its policy, its labelled cases and its recordings with content fingerprints, Verification for what real servers did, and Decisions for why the API is shaped as it is. The rustdoc is the reference for every type, at https://docs.rs/judgment (or `cargo doc --open`). The crate has been run against the hosted TypeSafe API (`jev-1.13.0`) and against Laya's open-weights server; its retry behaviour on 408, 429 and 529 is verified against wiremock only.

## Start here

- [README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/README.md): what the crate is for, what it guarantees, the walkthrough, the patterns and how to depend on it
- [CHANGELOG](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/CHANGELOG.md): what changed in each release, breaking changes listed
- [Full documentation text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/llms-full.txt): every page below, concatenated in this order

## Pages

- [judgment documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/index.md): Map of the judgment crate's documentation, what each page answers, and where the crate's documentation ends and an application's begins.
- [How judgment works](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/design.md): The two mechanisms the rustdoc cannot draw, typed handles from question to answer and the retry loop, with the response check, the error grouping, the request id and what the crate deliberately does not do.
- [What is in the crate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/tour.md): A tour of the crate's modules, question, answer, backend, client, http, error, eval, observer and contract, with the guarantee each one makes and the trade-off behind it, for a reader deciding where a concern belongs before opening the rustdoc.
- [Patterns](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/patterns.md): TypeSafe's four patterns, speculative fan-out, confidence-gated routing, composite scoring and intent routing, mapped onto the crate's types, with one runnable example each that replays committed recordings and three things the recordings teach about thresholds.
- [Testing without the model](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/testing.md): How an application tests its decisions with no key and no network, with the Fake backend that refuses an answer the question does not fit, the Recorder and Replay pair keyed by a content hash, and the eval module that grades recordings against labels.
- [The .jud format](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/jud.md): A YAML document format for a rubric with its policy, the labelled cases it is graded on and the recordings of what a model answered, with content fingerprints any implementation computes the same way; the specification, the reading rules and how the crate implements it.
- [Releasing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/releasing.md): How a version of the judgment crate is cut from its Conventional Commits with cocogitto, how the pushed tag publishes it to crates.io from CI, what to set up once, and what to do when a release goes wrong.

## Verification

- [How the crate is checked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/verification/method.md): The three checks that stand between the crate's mocks and a real server, the ignored live tests, the benchmark replay and the contract test against the vendored OpenAPI document, what each one can and cannot establish, and how to run them against the hosted API, Laya or Ollama.
- [Against the hosted TypeSafe API](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/verification/hosted-typesafe.md): The judgment crate's live tests run against api.typesafe.ai with a real key, what each one showed about the hosted wire that the mocks and the Laya run could not, what probing past the builder's limits taught (three 400 shapes, the token budget, non-determinism at two decimals, the confidence formulas) and what the crate changed for it, and how to repeat the check with one task.
- [Against Laya typed-decisions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/verification/laya-typed-decisions.md): How the judgment crate was tested against Laya's typed-decisions checkpoint through laya-serve, what each test asserts and why, the decoding bug the first run caught, the benchmark numbers, the 2026-10-03 re-run against laya-serve 0.3.24 and the legend comparison it loosened, and how to repeat the run.

## Research

- [System One client libraries](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/research/system-one-client-libraries.md): A survey of the twenty-five community Rust clients for the TypeSafe System One wire, the official Python and JavaScript SDKs and the live OpenAPI document, what each did that judgment 0.1 did not, the ranked changes worth making to the crate, the ones rejected and why, and what judgment 0.2.0 shipped of them.
- [Compatible servers and models](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/research/compatible-servers-and-models.md): The servers and models that speak the System One wire as of 2026-10-04, hosted and local, what the Jev Decision Index 0.2.1 says about how close the open ones are to Jev, what each one's limits and confidence semantics mean for a consumer of this crate, and which the crate has been run against or should be next.
- [Compared with the other Rust clients](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/research/client-comparison.md): A feature-by-feature comparison of judgment with the nine most-downloaded Rust crates for the System One wire, each read from its published source on 2026-10-04 and measured for dependency footprint and build time, in five grids (the wire, reading answers, resilience, testing and evaluation, observability and footprint), with what judgment should take from the others next.

## Decisions

- [Decisions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/decisions/README.md): The architecture decision records that govern the judgment crate's design, how they are numbered, how a record is written, and what has moved since each was accepted.
- [0003 Typed handles between questions and answers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/decisions/0003-typed-handles-between-questions-and-answers.md): Adding a question returns a handle that fixes the answer type, so the compiler ties each wire answer to the code that consumes it.
- [0013 Releases cut with cocogitto and published from CI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/decisions/0013-releases-cut-with-cocogitto-and-published-from-ci.md): The version is derived from Conventional Commits by cocogitto, the CHANGELOG stays hand-written, and a pushed tag runs the gate and publishes the crate to crates.io, so no release depends on one person's laptop or memory.
- [0014 A file format for rubrics, cases and recordings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chussenot/judgment/main/docs/decisions/0014-a-file-format-for-rubrics-cases-and-recordings.md): The questions a request sends, the policy that reads the answers, the labelled cases the policy is tuned on and the recordings of what a model answered get one YAML format, .jud, with the wire's own shapes, content fingerprints from RFC 8785 canonical JSON and strict reading, instead of staying in code, configuration and notebooks that drift apart.
